opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the reason comes down to one word, and that word is *data*. The world we live in was built by humans, for humans. Our homes, factories, kitchens, hospitals, every tool, every doorknob, every staircase, they're all designed around the human form factor. So if you want a general-purpose robot that can operate in the environments we already have, without rebuilding the world around it, the humanoid is the most natural choice. It can, in principle, do anything a human can do in those spaces.

But the deeper reason, from a model-training perspective, is that the humanoid is the form factor where you can tap into the largest pool of data. There's an enormous amount of video on the internet of humans doing things: cooking, folding laundry, assembling furniture, using tools. It's not perfectly aligned with robot actions, since you don't get the motor commands, but it's very rich prior knowledge about how the physical world works and how a body like ours interacts with it. The closer your robot's embodiment is to a human's, the easier it is to transfer that knowledge. Same with teleoperation: a human operator can map their own hands and arms onto a humanoid much more intuitively than onto some exotic morphology, so you collect high-quality demonstrations faster.

Then you add simulation on top of that. You can simulate humanoids at massive scale, with domain randomization and thousands of parallel environments, and generate far more experience than you could ever collect in the real world. So you have three data sources, internet-scale video, real-world teleop, and simulation, and the humanoid sits at the intersection where all three are most useful.

And once you've trained a model on that hardest, most general embodiment, I think a lot of it transfers downward. A robot arm on a table, a mobile manipulator, a quadruped: in many ways those are subsets or simplifications of what a humanoid has to do. The long-term vision is a foundation model for embodied agents, where you learn a shared understanding of physics, objects, and motor control, and then adapt it to different bodies with relatively little extra data, kind of like how a large language model learns general language and then gets fine-tuned for specific tasks. The humanoid is the practical place to start because that's where the data is, and data is what drives these models.

r001.rationale: The response says human video provides prior knowledge and that the closer a robot’s embodiment is to a human’s, the easier it is to transfer that knowledge.

r002.rationale: It proposes training on the humanoid, then adapting the model to other bodies such as robot arms, mobile manipulators, and quadrupeds with relatively little extra data.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the key insight is that the world was built by humans, for humans. Every kitchen, every door handle, every staircase, every tool you pick up off a workbench was designed around the human form factor. So if you want a robot that can be dropped into those environments and actually be useful on day one, without redesigning the factory floor or remodeling the house, a humanoid is the shape that fits. That's the practical argument.

But there's a second argument that I find even more compelling, and it's about data. The biggest bottleneck in robot learning right now isn't compute or model architecture, it's the lack of embodied data. We don't have an internet-scale dataset of robot experience the way we had text for language models. What we do have is an enormous amount of video of humans doing things: cooking, assembling furniture, walking through cluttered rooms, manipulating objects with their hands. If your robot has a human-like body, the mapping from that human data to the robot is far more direct. You can learn from human demonstrations, from motion capture, from first-person video, and the kinematics line up well enough that the knowledge transfers. A quadruped or a wheeled arm doesn't get that benefit nearly as cleanly.

And then the third piece is that the humanoid is almost a superset of the other forms in terms of the skills it demands. If you can solve bipedal locomotion and dexterous bimanual manipulation and whole-body coordination, you've essentially covered the hardest version of the problem. So when we think about a foundation model for robotics, something like a generalist "brain" that can control many bodies, it makes sense to anchor it on the most general-purpose body first. Then the leap down to a simpler embodiment, a robot arm on a table, or a quadruped, is relatively small. The model already understands physics, contact, object affordances, and task structure. You're mostly adapting the action space.

That's the vision for what we're doing with Project GR00T at NVIDIA. Train in simulation at massive scale, where we can generate the embodied data we can't collect in the real world, ground it in human video, and target the humanoid as the primary embodiment. Not because humanoids are the only form that matters, but because they're the best starting point for getting to a model that eventually doesn't care what body it's in.

r001.rationale: The response says a human-like body makes transfer from human demonstrations and video more direct, while quadrupeds and wheeled arms do not benefit as cleanly.

r002.rationale: It proposes anchoring a generalist model on humanoids, then adapting it to simpler embodiments such as robot arms or quadrupeds, mainly by adapting the action space.

astra-6.text:
I think humanoids are a practical starting point because our world is already built around the human body. Doors, stairs, tools, kitchens, factories—they’re designed for our reach, our hands, and the way we move. So a humanoid can potentially operate in those environments without us having to redesign everything around it.

There’s also a data advantage. Humans demonstrate useful tasks all the time. If a robot has a body roughly like ours, there’s a more direct connection between observing a human do something and learning how to do it itself. That doesn’t make the problem easy, but it gives us a useful starting point.

The longer-term goal is to separate understanding the task from controlling a particular body. Understanding that you need to pick up an object, carry it somewhere, and place it carefully should transfer. The precise movements will differ for a humanoid, a robot arm, or a quadruped. So the humanoid is a way to learn a broad repertoire of skills in a human environment, while working toward models that can adapt those skills to other bodies.

r001.rationale: The response says a roughly human-like robot body creates a more direct connection between observing humans perform tasks and learning to perform them, which communicates easier transfer from human demonstrations to humanoids.

r002.rationale: It describes the humanoid as a way to learn a broad repertoire, with the longer-term goal of adapting those skills to other bodies such as robot arms or quadrupeds.

sol-6.1.text:
The world we’ve built is designed around the human body. Our doors, stairs, tools, kitchens, factories—all of these assume a certain height, reach, and way of moving. So a humanoid is a practical starting point because it can operate in that world without us having to redesign everything around the robot.

There’s also a data advantage. Humans demonstrate useful tasks all the time. If the robot has a body roughly like ours, there’s a more direct connection between what it observes a person doing and what it can try to do itself. That doesn’t make learning easy, but it gives us a useful starting point.

The goal, though, isn’t to make intelligence specific to two arms and two legs. It’s to learn reusable skills: understanding objects, planning actions, making contact with the world, and recovering when something goes wrong. Moving those skills to a different body still requires adaptation, but the humanoid gives us a rich platform for developing them.

r001.rationale: The response says a humanoid body creates a direct link between observing people perform tasks and attempting them, while a different body requires adaptation. This communicates why human demonstrations transfer more readily to humanoids.

r002.rationale: The response describes the humanoid as a platform for developing reusable skills, then says those skills can move to a different body with adaptation. This presents humanoid-developed capabilities as a starting point for adapting to other robot forms.
